issues.subcategory: simulated data reported as empirical findings
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the abstract, methods, and results are based on randomized Qualtrics-generated dummy data, yet it presents statistical tests, p values, and substantive conclusions as if they were empirical findings. This invalidates all reported results and interpretations until real data are collected and analyzed.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.description: The participant section reports generated Qualtrics responses rather than actual recruited participants. A generated dataset cannot support claims about human behavior, intervention effects, or replication success.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between saying data are simulated and will be updated after data collection, saying data collection was launched, and saying data collection was completed before analyses. These mutually inconsistent statements make it impossible to determine whether the study is preregistered, ongoing, completed, or purely simulated.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.

issues.description: The manuscript claims data collection was completed before analyses, contradicting the repeated statements that the results are based on a randomized dummy dataset and will be updated after data collection.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.description: Participants selected their own intervention and identifiability conditions rather than being randomly assigned. This destroys the experimental design because observed differences can reflect participant preferences, prior beliefs, motivation, altruism, or other self-selection factors rather than the manipulations.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: causal effects inferred without random assignment
issues.description: The manuscript describes identifiability and intervention as independent variables and analyzes their effects, but if participants selected conditions, causal effects of identifiability or intervention cannot be estimated. Any group differences are confounded by selection into conditions.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.description: The design is described as within-subject, but the cell sizes and ANOVA degrees of freedom indicate a between-subjects 2 x 3 design with each participant contributing one observation. If the design was truly within-subject, repeated-measures or mixed-effects analyses and counterbalancing would be required; if it was between-subjects, the design description is wrong.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.subcategory: missing counterbalancing for claimed within-subject design
issues.description: Because the manuscript calls the study within-subject, participants would presumably see multiple victim/intervention conditions. No order randomization, counterbalancing, washout, or carryover control is reported. Such omissions would seriously bias responses in a within-subject design.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.description: The original dependent variable was an actual donation of real money. The replication uses an imaginary donation, which measures stated willingness rather than real giving behavior. Hypothetical charitable giving is vulnerable to social desirability and may not reproduce effects observed with real financial stakes.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original study gave participants money from a prior task and then allowed donation of that money. The replication removes this procedure, changing the psychological ownership, windfall, and real-cost structure of the donation decision.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: The manuscript states that participants donate to the corresponding victim(s), but in the joint condition it is unclear whether the donation is to the identified individual, the statistical victims, both, or the charity generally. This ambiguity undermines comparison with the original Study 3, where the critical question concerned donation to the identifiable victim after statistical information.
issues.quote: imaginary donation to corresponding victims across conditions

issues.subcategory: combining two original studies changes design
issues.description: The manuscript merges Studies 1 and 3 into one six-cell design. This is not a straightforward replication because the original studies tested different manipulations and designs separately. Combining them changes context, participant expectations, hypothesis structure, and estimands.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: explicit intervention added to joint condition
issues.description: The intervention is applied to the joint condition even though that was not part of the original Study 3 design. This creates a condition containing both explicit and implicit interventions and makes it difficult to isolate the mechanism of debiasing.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: The manuscript describes exposure to victim statistics in the joint condition as implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect. In the original theory, the joint condition was intended to evoke comparative or calculative evaluation, not to teach participants about the bias. Calling this learning conflates mechanism, manipulation, and outcome.
issues.quote: participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: changed estimand for identifiability main effect
issues.description: The replication analyzes identifiability as a three-level factor including the joint condition, whereas the original Study 1 main effect compared identifiable versus statistical victims. Adding the joint condition changes the omnibus test and makes it non-equivalent to the original effect being evaluated.
issues.quote: effect of identifiability on donation (with joint condition)

issues.description: The 2 x 3 ANOVA treats intervention and identifiability as orthogonal factors, but the joint condition itself is theorized as an implicit intervention. Thus the identifiability factor partly contains an intervention manipulation, and the intervention factor partly overlaps with explicit debiasing, making main effects difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: overclaiming close replication despite major deviations
issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as close to very close replication despite acknowledging different dependent-variable stimuli, different physical setting, different participant population, hypothetical rather than real donations, and modified intervention structure. This overstates comparability with the target article.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.description: The classification table labels the dependent-variable stimuli as different and physical/contextual variables as different, yet still concludes the study is close to very close replication. The stated deviations are too substantial to support that classification without stronger justification.
issues.quote: DV stimuli | Different

issues.description: The manuscript replaces the original victim information with updated Save the Children material but does not report the exact stimuli or show that they are equivalent in severity, vividness, emotionality, credibility, country, age, or wording. Stimulus differences may drive effects independently of identifiability.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.description: The manuscript relies on external links for the full survey and does not include exact wording, scale anchors, attention-check wording, manipulation text, victim stimuli, or donation question wording in the manuscript itself. This limits evaluation and replication, especially if links change or become inaccessible.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.description: The manuscript does not specify recruitment eligibility, location restrictions, language requirements, MTurk worker qualifications, prior participation filters, or whether the sample was U.S.-only. These details are necessary to evaluate comparability with the original study and generalizability.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: Participant compensation is not reported for the replication. Compensation affects MTurk sample quality, ethical review, motivation, attention, and comparability to the original real-money donation paradigm.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between saying the sample consists of Qualtrics-generated responses and saying participants will be recruited from Mechanical Turk. These are incompatible sources and imply different data-generating processes.
issues.quote: Medium (location) | Laboratory | Computer (online) | Computer (online)

issues.subcategory: MTurk source contradicted by generated response label
issues.description: The deviation table states that MTurk workers will be recruited, but the sample table describes the replication sample as Qualtrics-generated responses. This makes the actual or planned recruitment procedure unclear.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The manuscript says participants with prior knowledge and failed attention checks were excluded but does not report how many were excluded, whether exclusions occurred before or after randomization, or whether exclusions differed by condition. This prevents assessment of attrition bias.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: No procedure is reported for incomplete surveys, duplicate responses, item nonresponse, failed comprehension, speeders, or missing donation/feeling data. Missing-data decisions can substantially affect cell sizes, ANOVA results, and correlations.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration

issues.description: Excluding participants with prior knowledge or failed attention checks after condition exposure could create unequal attrition across conditions. The manuscript does not report whether exclusions were balanced across the six cells.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The study excludes people who know about the identifiable victim effect, yet the intervention itself involves teaching the effect. This creates an artificially restricted population and limits conclusions about whether deliberative knowledge reduces donation among real-world donors, some of whom may already know about such biases.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded

issues.description: The manuscript states that power analysis is in the supplement but does not report the planned alpha level, target effect, power, allocation ratio, expected exclusions, or whether the design was powered for interactions, simple effects, correlations, and extension analyses. Readers cannot evaluate whether N = 1000 is justified for the modified six-cell design.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.description: Although total N is 1000, the six-cell design leaves approximately 159 to 175 participants per cell. This may be underpowered for the original Study 3 small effect and for interactions, moderated effects, and extension tests, especially after exclusions.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate model for bounded ordinal donation outcome
issues.description: Donation is a bounded discrete response from 0 to 5 dollars. The original included ordered probit models, but the replication drops them and relies on ANOVA without reporting distributional diagnostics, robustness checks, or models appropriate for ordinal/censored bounded outcomes.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The manuscript reports ANOVAs but does not report checks or remedies for normality, homoscedasticity, influential observations, bounded-scale nonnormality, or unequal cell sizes. These assumptions matter for donation and Likert-type feeling variables.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.description: The analysis plan performs some post-hoc tests only if omnibus tests are significant. Such conditional analysis rules should be clearly preregistered and justified because they create researcher degrees of freedom and affect error rates.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test   (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.subcategory: multiple testing not controlled across outcome families
issues.description: The manuscript tests donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, post-hoc comparisons, and six correlations. Only selected pairwise comparisons use Bonferroni correction; there is no correction or multiplicity strategy across the full family of outcomes and hypotheses, increasing false-positive risk.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.description: The study conducts separate correlations between aggregated feelings and donation in six conditions without correcting for multiple testing or using a single interaction model to compare associations across conditions.
issues.quote: correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across six different conditions (statistical/intervention, statistical/no intervention, identifiable/intervention, identifiable/no intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.description: The manuscript says affective feelings predict donation, but feelings were measured after the donation decision. Post-decision self-reports may reflect rationalization of the donation rather than antecedent causes, so causal or predictive language is not warranted without temporal ordering or experimental manipulation of feelings.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: The aggregated feelings variable combines affective states with moral responsibility and donation appropriateness, which are evaluative or normative judgments rather than emotions. No reliability, factor analysis, or theoretical justification for aggregation is reported.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: perceived impact mislabeled as affective feeling
issues.description: Perceived impact is an efficacy appraisal, not an affective feeling. Treating it as a feeling variable conflates affective and cognitive constructs and complicates interpretation of aggregated or segregated feeling analyses.
issues.quote: We aim to extend the replication study by considering the “perceived impact of donation” as one of the feeling variables indicated in Small et al. (2007)’s Study 1.

issues.subcategory: extension does not test proposed mechanism
issues.description: The manuscript motivates perceived impact as linked to donation and the identifiable victim effect, but the stated hypothesis only tests whether perceived impact differs by victim condition. It does not test whether perceived impact predicts donation, mediates identifiability effects, or explains debiasing.
issues.quote: This highlights the importance of how the perceived impact of donation is linked with the identifiable victim effect in this replication. It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: no manipulation check for deliberative thinking
issues.description: The central construct is deliberative or analytical thinking, but the manuscript does not report any manipulation check showing that the explicit or implicit intervention actually increased deliberation, analytical reasoning, or calculative thought.
issues.quote: The research conducted by Small et al. (2007) showed that the identifiable victim effect could be eliminated by deliberative thinking, meaning that thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation to offer assistance to a single beneficiary.

issues.subcategory: demand characteristics in explicit debiasing manipulation
issues.description: Teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect before asking for donations can reveal the hypothesis and create demand characteristics or social desirability effects. The manuscript does not report any demand assessment, suspicion probe, or control for hypothesis awareness.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims.

issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen's d for factorial ANOVA main effects and especially for an interaction effect without explaining the contrast or conversion. A factorial interaction is not naturally summarized by a simple two-group d unless a specific contrast is defined.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: original Study 1 degrees of freedom inconsistent
issues.description: The original Study 1 is reported as N = 121 with a 2 x 2 design, but Table 1 gives residual df = 115 while Table 11 gives df = 117 for a contrast. The manuscript does not explain missing data, covariates, or why degrees of freedom differ.
issues.quote: Effect of identifiability and intervention on donation (Study 1) (N=121)

issues.description: The manuscript reports Study 3 means but omits standard deviations and residual degrees of freedom, preventing independent verification of effect sizes, confidence intervals, and power calculations.
issues.quote: Statistical victim | 1.14 | N/A | 2 | N/A | 5.67 | <.01** | .07

issues.subcategory: post-hoc donation means contradict descriptive table
issues.description: The text states that statistical-victim participants donated more than identifiable-victim participants, but the descriptive table implies the opposite when averaging across intervention cells. This indicates either reversed labels, incorrect post-hoc output, or erroneous interpretation.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: From Table 7, identifiable-victim donation averages approximately 2.54 across intervention levels, while statistical-victim donation averages approximately 2.25. The narrative reverses these values, undermining the reported conclusion.
issues.quote: Identifiable victim condition | Statistical victim condition | Joint condition

issues.subcategory: post-hoc t, d, and CI inconsistent
issues.description: In Table 10, t(994) = -2.40 with approximately equal groups of over 300 participants implies a Cohen's d around -0.18, not 0.076. The sign of t is also inconsistent with the positive d. The confidence interval for d includes zero while the Bonferroni-adjusted p is reported as significant, suggesting calculation or reporting errors.

In Table 14, t(994) = 2.47 and the reported means differ by 0.27 with SDs around 1.4, implying d around 0.19 to 0.20, not 0.08. The reported confidence interval includes zero despite a significant Bonferroni-adjusted p value, indicating inconsistent statistics.

issues.subcategory: original contrast t sign inconsistent with means
issues.description: The original contrast table reports the identifiable/no-intervention mean as higher than other conditions but gives a negative t value. Unless the contrast was defined in the reverse direction, the sign is inconsistent and should be clarified.
issues.quote: Identifiable/ no intervention | 2.83 | 2.10 | 117 | -4.06 | N/A | N/A | <.001***

issues.description: The introduction hypothesizes higher perceived impact for identifiable victims, but the abstract claims people have lower perceived impact when facing an identifiable victim or identifiable victim with statistics. These are opposite predictions or interpretations.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: abstract conclusion unsupported by reported extension results
issues.description: The abstract says perceived impact is lower for identifiable and identifiable-with-statistics conditions, but the reported post-hoc test finds only a difference between statistical and joint conditions, not between identifiable and statistical victims.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: analytical-reasoning conclusion conflicts with interaction result
issues.description: The abstract states there is no empirical support for analytical reasoning affecting the identifiable victim effect, but the reported ANOVA shows a significant identifiability-by-intervention interaction on donation. The manuscript does not reconcile this apparent contradiction.
issues.quote: found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.description: After finding a significant interaction, the manuscript conducts a single contrast comparing identifiable/no-intervention with all other five conditions combined. This contrast does not directly test the theoretically relevant simple effects, such as whether intervention reduces donation specifically within the identifiable condition but not the statistical condition.
issues.quote: we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of  identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.subcategory: pooled contrast combines conceptually distinct cells
issues.description: Combining statistical/no-intervention, statistical/intervention, identifiable/intervention, joint/intervention, and joint/no-intervention into one comparison group obscures theoretically distinct effects and may cancel or mask condition-specific patterns. It is not equivalent to the original targeted contrast once the joint conditions are added.

The manuscript mentions JAMOVI and R but does not provide software versions, R packages, exact functions, contrast coding, sums-of-squares type, or CI calculation method. These details are necessary to reproduce ANOVA and effect-size results.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.description: The reported confidence intervals for eta-squared and Cohen's d are not clearly defined, sometimes include zero despite significant p values, and lack methods for computation. This raises concerns about effect-size reporting accuracy.

The manuscript treats moral responsibility and donation appropriateness as affective reactions, but these are moral/evaluative judgments. Combining them with upset, sympathy, and touched blurs distinct constructs and weakens interpretation of affective mechanisms.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: scale anchors and item wording absent
issues.description: The manuscript reports means for feelings and perceived impact but does not provide the response scale, anchors, item wording, number of items, scoring direction, or reliability. Without these, the measurement properties of the dependent variables cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: Table 8 Descriptive statistics for aggregated feelings across conditions

issues.subcategory: correlational mediation implied but not tested
issues.description: The manuscript discusses affective feelings and perceived impact as mechanisms of donation behavior, but the analyses are correlations and mean comparisons. No mediation model, temporal ordering, or experimental manipulation of the mediator is provided, so mechanistic claims are not supported.
issues.quote: The second goal of the current research is to examine the effect of affective feelings on the studied phenomenon, with the introduction of an extension known as the perceived impact of donation.

issues.subcategory: overgeneralized claims about humans and people
issues.description: The manuscript makes broad claims about human tendencies and prosocial motivation despite using either a simulated dataset or a planned online MTurk sample with unspecified geography. Such claims exceed the sample and design.
issues.quote: The identifiable victim effect is the human’s tendency to offer greater support to an identifiable individual over a larger group of anonymous victims represented by numerical statistics

issues.description: The target study used a U.S. laboratory/student-center context, while the replication geography is not specified. Cultural differences in charitable giving, familiarity with Save the Children, income, and norms may moderate effects, but this is not addressed.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: online setting changes control over procedure
issues.description: Moving from a laboratory/student-center setting with real money and a charity letter to an online survey changes attention, privacy, perceived realism, experimenter presence, and donation credibility. The manuscript acknowledges the setting change but does not address how it may affect the effect under replication.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The manuscript states that supplementary materials contain comparisons and deviations, but the main text does not clearly distinguish preregistered confirmatory analyses from exploratory extensions, deviations, and post-hoc decisions. This impairs assessment of researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: For more details about the deviation from the original study, please refer to the supplementary session of “Comparisons and deviations”.

issues.description: Key information including power analysis, design table, procedures, comparisons, deviations, and open-science disclosures is repeatedly deferred to external documents. A reader cannot evaluate the manuscript as a standalone report, and external links may not be stable or peer-reviewed.
issues.quote: Power analyses and all materials used in these experiments are available in the supplementary materials.

issues.description: The manuscript attributes identifiable-victim responses to the availability heuristic, but the proposed mechanism is more directly affect, vividness, singularity, or evaluability. The link between availability and valuation of a personalized individual is asserted rather than theoretically developed or measured.
issues.quote: The “availability heuristic”  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.description: The introduction claims the identifiable victim effect demonstrates unfairness and inefficient resource allocation. The current experiment measures hypothetical donations to victims, not fairness judgments, social welfare, or allocation efficiency, so these broader claims are not directly supported.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation

issues.subcategory: original Study 3 d for three-level ANOVA unclear
issues.description: The manuscript reports a single Cohen's d for the effect in Study 3, which had three conditions. A three-level omnibus effect is not adequately summarized by one d unless a specific pairwise contrast is defined.
issues.quote: In Study 3, the effect of implicitly activating the analytical thinking mechanism on donation was d = 0.23, 95% CI [0.01, 0.45], regarded as a small effect.

issues.description: The sample comparison table appears to contain duplicated replication columns and duplicated values, making it unclear what sample is being compared and whether N = 1000 is before or after exclusions.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.description: The manuscript involves charitable donation decisions, deception-like demand manipulations, online participants, and possible exclusions, but does not report IRB/ethics approval, informed consent, debriefing, data privacy, or whether real donations are made.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s)

issues.description: The manuscript excludes participants who failed an attention check but does not report the item, placement, criteria, whether it was preregistered, or whether it was independent of the manipulation. Attention-check exclusions can bias samples if not transparently handled.
issues.quote: as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The study excludes participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect but does not report how this was assessed, when it was asked, or what response criteria triggered exclusion. If assessed after the intervention, it may be contaminated by the manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded

issues.subcategory: lack of planned model for unequal cell sizes
issues.description: Cell sizes differ across conditions, yet the manuscript does not state whether Type I, II, or III sums of squares were used in the factorial ANOVAs. With unequal cell sizes, sums-of-squares choice affects main-effect and interaction tests.

issues.subcategory: donation appropriateness as dependent affective outcome
issues.description: Donation appropriateness may be a normative judgment about the correct action rather than an affective reaction. Treating it as a feeling outcome can obscure whether the intervention affects emotion, moral reasoning, perceived efficacy, or compliance with perceived norms.
issues.quote: donation appropriateness

issues.subcategory: intervention effect language unsupported by dummy/self-selected data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly refers to the effect of intervention on donation, but the reported data are simulated and the procedure says participants selected conditions. Therefore intervention-effect language is not justified.
issues.quote: Summary of statistical tests for identifiability and intervention on donation
